title: Why Enterprise AI Adoption Is Slower Than You Think — Aaron Levie (Box) + Harrison Chase

segments.text: >> Thank you so much for being here.
>> Thank you.
I think my last time I was in this building was like a rave.
Has anybody been to like an EDM show here before?
Raise your hand.
We have a couple.
We were probably the same one.
>> We were talking about that before.
>> Oh, really?
>> I think a lot of folks in our team have been here mostly for that.
>> This is a very familiar venue.
I was doing some research on you before looking at your tweets.
You're a prolific tweeter.
How do you do it?
It's funny.
Prolific tweeter is sort of one of these backhanded compliments.
No, it's a full-on compliment.
OK, it's like, do you want to be a prolific tweeter?
I don't know.
I basically just tweet what we're running into at Box
and what we're seeing when we're building agents and working on
AI — what I'm hearing from customers, from the market, and from whatever is in
the zeitgeist that sort of resonates.
So unfortunately it's a pretty boring framework.
It's just like, you know, a couple times a day, whatever I think is happening in the
world.
It's a couple times a day, but it's a bunch of paragraphs and it's all spot on, like
very in tune with what's going on in the ecosystem.
I'm in awe.
Thank you.
I mean, I think most people know how to write, so you can all try this at home.
So just try and type a couple paragraphs
and just see what happens.
It's so funny because I definitely got a C plus, probably,
in English in high school.
But everybody thinks that I write a lot.
And I was like, I don't know.
You can either write an email or write a tweet.
Might as well write a tweet.
Do you use AI for your tweets at all?
No.
All right.
Well, I think you're definitely one of the most--
And some of my tweets make it very obvious,
because I'll look at it later,
and oh my god, there are actually like up to nine mistakes
in this tweet between grammar and spelling.
So it's definitely like proof of human work.
- Yeah, you almost have to add that in on purpose
so people know it's not AI.
- Yep, in this case, it happens fully organically, so.
- I think you're one of the smartest people
in terms of what it takes for enterprises
to actually adopt AI.
And I imagine this is because you work
with a number of them daily.
What advice would you have for enterprises
who are thinking about this?
I imagine everyone's thinking about this.
- Yeah, and I think —
just to point back to the first question —
I'm super lucky because this has been true
basically since the founding of the company.
You guys live, I think the same world,
probably many folks live in this world as well.
We get to be in the tech industry, in Silicon Valley,
sort of seeing the breakthroughs of what's happening
in AI today, but previously it was for us,
it was cloud computing initially.
that we had when we started Box,
which was there's these breakthroughs happening in tech,
and in this case it was the early days of cloud
and cloud infrastructure and all that,
but to translate that to the regular knowledge worker
or regular enterprise, there has to be some bridge.
You have to have simple interfaces,
they have to be usable by end users.
There's got to be a way to package up this infrastructure
in a way that makes sense for use cases.
And with AI, we're seeing the same thing —
incredible breakthroughs happening
Model progress is absolutely insane.
Infrastructure and framework and the kind of surrounding
scaffolding is kind of progressing at an incredible rate.
But most enterprises in the world
have to have some kind of bridge of how
do I get access to this in a way that's
relevant to my use cases and to my organization.
So I get to spend a lot of time with
especially large enterprises,
but businesses of all sizes across industries.
And we get to kind of see like what's happening
in their organizations as they go and adopt AI
and as they try and bring all this amazing technology
to their organization.
I think it's probably what everybody here is experiencing,
whether you're building a product for the enterprise
or you're in an enterprise yourself.
And maybe it can be netted out to this:
we have this insane progress we're seeing
in things like AI coding in particular.
We're all using agents for developing code,
and we all see every day the full potential of what happens
when an agent can run loose on a large task
and a large project.
And then we look at the rest of knowledge work
and marketing and sales and finance and research.
And the big question is, can we get those similar gains
in all those other parts of the organization
in these business processes that are in domain-specific
or industry-specific areas?
And that's the main question that I think
is on the mind of every single enterprise, right?
We all as technologists are using this in our daily lives.
Our colleagues that are maybe not in tech
are using it in their daily lives, but more for a chat,
sort of basic interaction.
So the big question is when and how
do we get these full, agentic workflows deployed
across the rest of knowledge work?
That's kind of the topic that takes up the mind share
of I think most enterprises today.
And again, some of it is then building this internally,
figuring out how to do it.
Some of it is working with partners and vendors
and providers to make that happen.
- Yeah, I mean, on that,
like what is the answer to that question?
What is working?
- I purposely left it rhetorical
because I think we're figuring it out.
But the tricky thing is —
I don't know how much this will resonate —
'cause I think being in tech,
so many people here, it's like you have to kind of step out
for a second and think about this.
Like, when you think about the full amazing power of AI
coding agents, it has sort of like every great property
going for it, right?
The models themselves are hyper-trained on code,
because that's a plentiful content type on the internet.
The work itself is verifiable, so you
kind of know if the code worked.
And so that helps both in the RL process
and the actual kind of when you're using the agent
to do some work.
The users are hyper-technical by definition.
And so when the agent does something and it goes wrong,
you know how to fix it.
Or if it says I need access to a data source,
you generally have the ability to get the right MCP server
involved in that workflow.
You know that when you're in a coding agent
and it's like, hey, I need to download this CLI
from this vendor in this package,
you have the wherewithal to say yes or no
based on that situation.
I was, as a brief aside, my dad has gotten into coding,
but he's not historically a coder.
He is kind of good at Excel and data science stuff.
And I was just watching him use Claude code,
and he was just like, yes, download that package,
and yes, and like, for sure, for sure,
his computer now is full of malware.
Like, there's just no chance.
Every NPM attack we've seen in the past three days,
like he's got every one of those.
So — sorry, Dad, wherever you are —
this is what a lot of teams adjacent
to engineers are gonna experience
and then imagine if you're even more adjacent
and you're like just in, you know,
you're in marketing and you're in sales,
all of that kind of technical complexity.
And that's a real problem.
And then you actually have a kind of a pesky problem
that is so boring to talk about,
but it's just so real.
When you're an engineer, you generally have access — via the codebase —
to most of the data and context
to work within for whatever you're working on.
And permission structures on codebases
generally are fairly wide open because you just 187 00:07:39,800 --> 00:07:41,820 need access to the codebase to do whatever you're doing.
In knowledge work, that's just not the case.
Every single individual and every single team
within an enterprise has a different permutation--
different permutations of what data they can access.
And so by definition, agents also
have those same permutations, which
just multiplies the complexity of when an agent goes
and does a task.
So think about all those things that we just said.
So the work is not as verifiable as code.
The models are still working on getting better
at these non-coding domain tasks.
The users are not as technical,
so getting
the full universe of things they need to plug in
to make these agents work is obviously harder.
And they don't have access to all the data they need
often to do the work that they need.
And so agents, again, inherit that same level
of lack of access, which means that, you know,
as a knowledge worker, you can just go around
and say, "Hey Sally,
can you give me access to that thing?"
But an agent doesn't have that same ability
to navigate that complex paradigm of like, well,
what does an agent do when it runs into a limit of what
it has access to?
So this is the gap.
And so the question is: how are we,
as an industry,
going to bridge that gap?
And so I think you're starting to see some of the makings
of examples of where this might work.
So first of all, highly domain and vertical specific agent
startups are emerging.
And that's one great thing, because now you can basically
say, you know what, we can deliver this in a really
kind of purpose-built way.
So we can dramatically reduce all of the issues on, how do
you get the context of the agent?
Well, we know the domain, so we already have a leg up on that.
How do you get the right data to the agent?
Well, here are the set of MCP connectors that we're already
going to work with.
There's usually some version of a forward-deployed engineer
in that workflow.
So already you have people that are going to be wired to that vertical that can help support that.
So I think on the startup side, I think this creates an incredible opportunity if you're doing domain and vertical specific, you know, agent work.
And then on the enterprise side, it's another sort of advantage which is you understand your enterprise better than any outside vendor.
So it also creates an opportunity for how do you go and bridge these agents and this technology into your organization.
And that's another set of, I think, roles and interesting
opportunities that we're starting to see emerge, which is,
like, OK, does your technology team have an AI agent
sort of internal forward deployed engineer?
And how are they setting these things up?
So that's a little bit of the early things that we're seeing.
But I think we have to be in for many, many years
of diffusion of this technology.
And we're going to have this huge cognitive dissonance
between the extreme capability of AI coding agents
that just are continuing to go hyperbolic
versus what we're gonna do in the rest of knowledge work
because of all those issues that I mentioned.
And we're just gonna be in for years and years
of deployment and change management and adoption
and that's I think what we all have to kind of
collectively sign up for.
And oh by the way, it's just a brief asterisk.
It's also why the doomers are generally gonna be wrong
on the takeoff because of the sort of rate of diffusion
of how this is gonna actually enter organizations.
- How are you guys at Box thinking
of tackling that with Box agent?
So that seems to me to be horizontal,
but you're already building upon a pretty solid data layer.
And so how are you guys thinking about that?
And how are you thinking about bridging the gap?
- Yeah, so I think we're a little bit
in this quasi-interesting territory
'cause we're horizontal.
So we don't have the level of domain specifics of insurance
and banking and legal, et cetera.
The thing that we have domain understanding on
is enterprise content at a horizontal level
and how to work with things like file systems
and how to handle all the ways that agents and models need
to understand working with our file system
and working with enterprise content.
And how do you create a pipeline of making sure
your data is sort of ready for agents in a secure way,
in a well-governed way, with the right access controls
and the right sort of security and governance on that.
And so we do a lot of things well before we even
think about AI to get enterprise content
or unstructured data ready for AI.
So we have a whole document conversion pipeline
that turns your content into a variety of file formats
that agents work well with.
We also do a lot in the
security and access controls area.
So that's a lot of the kind of core plumbing.
And then with the BoxAgent,
its job is to be an expert
at working with enterprise content.
And then it needs, obviously, the context of that workflow.
So it's going to need either skills or custom agent knowledge —
what is your business
process?
What are you trying to automate?
And that looks like, I think, anybody else's agent
that you'd go build.
Or we'll plug into a broader agent.
So via our MCP server, we'll plug into a Harvey or a Claude
for legal.
And then that will obviously take on the domain-specific
sort of understanding.
- You had a lot of this core plumbing
around permissions and governance before agents.
Have you seen that it's changed because of agents?
- Yeah, there are a bunch of things
that we've benefited from — sometimes
we got lucky, like we made an architectural decision
10 years ago that we obviously made it for people,
but we equally get the same kind of gains
within a world of agents.
Like most companies, we've had
our deeply religious battles on things like:
which JavaScript framework to go with,
and which database to use,
and that's obviously the classic engineering battle
that would happen.
We had years and years of those same kind of
incredibly intense battles on things like,
how do you design a file system,
and how should the permissions architecture work?
And so we benefited from incredibly intense
sort of processes and ways of making decisions
to ensure that we had the most amount of flexibility.
Again, more for people use cases,
sometimes for application use cases,
but now we're benefiting from the fact
that agents get all of those benefits as well.
So within Box as an example,
there's not two ways you can store files.
There's only one way you can store files.
There's only one canonical ID
for every object in the system.
There's only one governance model.
So we, you know, versus many of our kind of,
maybe legacy competitors where there's like three different
ways that data could show up in the system.
It's a single file system, it's a single governance model,
a single permissions architecture.
So agents get the benefit of all of that.
Then there's some areas where we've realized,
oh, we probably do have to evolve the platform.
Our search engine needs to take in different signals
because the agent can now consume 100 times
the search results as a human.
So if it can consume 100 times the search results
as a person, then you might need to rank things differently
or maybe ranking is less important
than just context in the search results
because then the agent can do its own ranking.
So we've had to do a bunch of tweaks
to our search engine as one example.
We've had to do a bunch of things
where in our document pipeline,
we have to convert data in an agent-ready format.
So we have an API now that will take
basically any content type and turn it into markdown.
So some things that just make it so our agent
or any external agent can work with this data much better.
- You mentioned before that you have an agent inside of Box
and you expose that via MCP.
And I think you guys also have just regular search endpoints
over MCP as well.
As you think about company strategy —
do you have a strong opinion of how much you want people
to be consuming box AI in the box AI interface
versus via MCP?
- We have sort of like what we wish would happen
and then we're also realists.
Being in enterprise software,
you kind of know that ultimately the customer's gonna win.
There's very few companies that can kind of hold out
from overall customer trends and whatever
that kind of mega trend is.
So I think, and this is probably something
that every single one of the software players
has to face right now, which is,
when does your agent experience show up
versus when are you headless?
And even headless takes on two forms,
'cause it could be our AI being headless,
or it could just be our regular APIs being headless.
And so that has its own kind of set of dimensions to it.
But the way we think about it:
we have to get insanely good in our harness at things
where working with content is the most important thing,
where being token efficient is the most important thing,
where having the right choice of models
is the most important thing.
We've got to be the best at that when
it deals with enterprise content.
So we have, for instance, an agent that just
does document extraction.
And we'd like to think that document agent
will beat any horizontal system
that you could send that problem to
because we're just hyper wired to that.
We have our own evals for that.
We only work on that problem.
Conversely, if you're just working with, you know,
Claude Cowork or some other or ChatGPT
and you want to have content show up
inside of that experience,
then we know that that's going to be 100% headless
and that'll be driven by whatever
the customer decides to roll out to their organization.
And we are completely indifferent philosophically
to either of those approaches that the customer wants to do.
I think that's what we all are going
to have to sign up for if you're building software,
is you should just expect that you should create
a world-class experience within your product,
and you should create world-class APIs
that any external system can interact with.
And by volume of system usage,
it's mostly going to be headless.
But for people doing a bunch of work, they'll often be in your interface or agent directly.
- Yeah, Salesforce recently exposed all their APIs headless — and that's definitely—
- And that was a pretty big symbolic moment. The world's largest SaaS company fully endorsing that headless is the future.
I've already used their headless MCP a ton of times for ways that previously, interestingly,
this is the bull case for all of this, I've used their MCP server now for tasks that were
both more complex and much higher volume than what I ever would have had an internal analyst
go do.
And this is the Jevons paradox of all this —
there are lots of things where, when you're inside a workplace
and you know,
that's a person who's going to spend
five or three hours on this project —
Is that really the most important thing for them
to go do versus everything else that they're gonna work on
whereas with an agent I don't care, other than the token costs.
So I give tasks to a variety of agents all the time
that I wouldn't have asked a person to do,
but it ends up doing useful work for me.
And so Salesforce MCP server is a great example
where I'll just hand off some market research,
and it'll go and do maybe 20 minutes of work
that would have been the equivalent of hours of human work
that I just absolutely would not have ever
had somebody else go and do.
And that's the example of now the new surplus
of what we're gonna start to see
is you'll just use these systems, 10x or 100x more,
depending on how valuable that data is
or where it shows up as being value-creative for the organization.
- Yeah, that's interesting that you say that,
'cause I think there is a bunch of fear
around being headless and getting disintermediated
or having other people drive it,
but it seems like it's just driving more usage.
- I think there's some areas where I can appreciate the fear.
There's not a perfect quadrant,
maybe you guys could publish one
so we could all like know what's gonna happen,
but there's probably a framework of:
is this type of data
sitting on top of unsaturated
use cases in the enterprise?
Like if that data could be unleashed at like,
you know, for everything, how much more would it get used?
Versus there are some data sources where,
where no, like even if you could throw
any amount of compute at that,
I just don't need to do more with that information.
And I think
we haven't yet figured out how to parse
what types of systems could you really use,
you know, a ton more versus which ones
are kind of already meeting their set of needs with.
And that will help us figure out
what things are a huge opportunity versus
just neutral.
You talked a little bit about your harness
for knowledge work and document intelligence.
We also talked about coding agents
and how those are taking off pretty rapidly.
How much do you look at coding agent harnesses
for inspiration around what your harness should look like
and how similar do you think they'll end up being
in the long term?
Yeah — and what you guys are doing with Deep
Deep Agents is to me right on point.
because if you think about it,
and I was late to this conclusion,
and I've only sort of seen the light
maybe in the past six months on this,
but I think you guys were super early
and a bunch of folks were early,
which is like these agents will always be better at code
than probably everything else.
So if they're always better at code than everything else,
then we should probably start to use that as an advantage
in everything that we're doing agentically.
And guess what?
It turns out that if you're really good at code,
then you're probably also really good at tool use
using MCPs and writing code on the fly
to perform some kind of action.
So we should probably take advantage of that.
And this is an imperfect analogy,
but to some extent it's sort of like,
what if every knowledge worker or domain in a business
had an unlimited supply of engineers
right next to them to do whatever they are trying to do,
now essentially for free,
turns out it's becoming probably more expensive than people.
But we thought it was free.
So we need to figure that part out.
So God bless Nvidia for that problem.
But basically, if you imagine your social media manager,
or your performance marketer, or your sales system analyst,
if they had an engineer full time next to them,
what would they have them go do?
Well, you'd probably say: I'm going to
wire up the most wild automated marketing campaign.
I'm going to pull the best customer intelligence from all my data systems
and surface it to my sales rep.
So what are those?
Those are coding tasks that, if we had expendable engineering resources
previously, you could have put an engineer on that and you just never would have because
we don't have expendable coders in organizations.
But now you do.
And so the idea of take a code harness,
make it really, really good now at non-coding tasks.
I mean, they're coding, but they're not for engineers.
They're for knowledge work.
That kind of becomes an interesting primitive
that sort of makes sense across all of knowledge work.
And oh, by the way, we're now seeing this with Codex
as a super app, or seeing this with Claude Cowork.
And until proven otherwise,
harnesses now
make sense to be these expert more than just coders.
They should have a computer.
They should have a sandbox.
They can write code and run code in.
They actually obviously need connectors
to all the different systems that they're using.
And then there's an overlay of what makes them
more than just coders.
And that's either the vertical or horizontal domain
expertise.
So in our world, we spend a lot of time in our system prompt
and the various parts of the harness.
We spend time making sure that our agent knows
about file systems.
How do you peruse a file system,
and when should you use a search tool
versus when should you navigate a folder path?
And it's like a really interesting problem
Because if you just searched every single time,
then often search doesn't tell you the surrounding
environment that something might be within.
But clicking a couple folders deep,
you all of a sudden get that information.
And so you actually need to know like what is the type
of task I'm being given and should I be doing a search
to find the single document or should I be going
through a folder tree to find the sort of workspace
that everything lives within.
And so we spent a lot of time to make our agent really good
at those types of things.
And then obviously that needs to then show up
in a vertical specific way, because you
can build a custom agent and so on.
But I think everybody is going to have some form of that.
But it will be basically built on the backbone
of a coding harness.
As you guys think about building these agents,
how do you think about model selection choice for what to use?
And do you use multiple models in one agent run
when I'm interacting with BoxAgent?
Will it call multiple under the hood?
We do with some asterisks.
There are some penalties,
like with prompt caching.
And so it's like, I think we're trying to figure out
even what's our best version of hybrid on that.
But I do think this is going to be a fun back-and-forth
ping-pong in the industry right now — on one hand,
you could go to a harness that is sort of purpose
built for a model.
And by definition of its purpose built for a model,
the model provider
is going to be more oriented toward token maximization,
not even necessarily in an explicit way
— they just wouldn't inherently care
to make it token-efficient,
since that's not core to their business model.
And obviously, it's gonna be wired up
against effectively one model.
And so, for everybody who's not a frontier lab,
you're probably doing things intentionally to be multi-model.
And if you're multi-model, what are the benefits?
One, different capabilities from the models
then become useful.
So one model is better at coding, another is better
at legal contracts, another model is better at looking
at an insurance claim document.
OK, once you have evals, you can kind of know that.
So that gives you one advantage of being neutral,
is sort of capability differentiation.
There's a performance differentiation
because I can be like, okay, Gemini Flash is faster
than Opus 4, and so there are some things
that you just want different types of workloads
being applied against, and then there's finally cost,
and cost might become the big story in the next three years.
And so if cost becomes the really big story
in the next three years, then what's gonna happen
is actually sending these tasks
to the most general purpose system
is going to basically average out your costs.
Sometimes you'll
do it efficiently because it just
happens to align with that system.
And sometimes you'll be spending way too much money
for that task.
And so I don't know when and how this happens,
but there's some threshold-- another graph you guys
should publish.
It's a great idea.
Yeah, I was taking notes.
I don't know if they are.
They'll probably be like your worst tweets.
There's probably some threshold where the cost savings
of the task become worth having a dedicated harness to.
And we're all kind of figuring out where those points are.
So if you were to go do an insurance claims process,
and you were going to go and automate that as much
as possible and either generate $50 million more per year
or cost $50 million per year, but it's either big upside
or big costs, then probably there's
some point in the threshold where it'd be better for you
to be hyper tuned to the right model,
the right capability, the right custom instructions
for that workload.
And because that could net tens of millions of dollars
of either more revenue or more cost savings.
And so not every workflow has that.
Me just chatting and trying to figure out
like how do I summarize the document
doesn't really have that component,
but a really heavy duty workflow will.
And I think that will mean that over time,
as you have frontier intelligence
that will always be expensive,
And you can peel off
just frontier minus one intelligence
from like three months ago.
Then all of a sudden, it starts to make sense
to peel those kind of workloads probably to cheaper models,
where there's some kind of capability maybe focus.
And you then ultimately would want to harness
that could kind of handle that level of sort of neutrality.
And that I think will be an interesting trend
to watch what happens, what parts of an industry
will that happen in, et cetera.
I think this is already happening over the past few months.
I think there was the Uber CTO who said they blew through all
their token budget.
I think ServiceNow recently said something similar.
I think you had a tweet on token budgeting.
I think it's happening with coding agents first,
because I think adoption is first and foremost.
But then once everyone starts adopting these frontier models,
costs explode.
What do you think the end game for that
is in coding in particular?
You guys running into that at Box at all?
Are you seeing this pretty commonly in enterprises?
- Yeah, the
token-maxing meme only lasted about three days
because, first of all,
only Facebook can actually afford to do that.
And sure,
some very well-funded startups here
can do it too — but
for us mere mortal companies, we have to have budgets
and planning cycles around
how much we can use.
And so we have not yet run into like major existential issues
on the coding side, we're still more in the ascent,
like where we're just continuing to say,
yeah, use it as much as you can, assuming it's productive,
but we're not rewarding you for using lots of tokens
because you just get weird, obviously,
perverse incentives on that.
So it's just like, use it productively.
And then we use our roadmap really as a means
of pushing the envelope.
So we want to stack more things into the roadmap,
and that should actually control
and drive the token utilization.
But I do think that as this sort of translates
into enterprises, and there's a real difference if you're
at a Silicon Valley-funded startup —
you can convert VC dollars into tokens —
but a Wall Street bank
or a public company — name your industry —
can't do that.
They have EPS targets, they have to hit every single quarter.
And so they can't all of a sudden spend $10 million more
on an AI bill.
And so once that pressure starts to build,
all of a sudden you need to
do things more efficiently,
which means we probably need a mixture of models
in these types of workflows,
and that's just gonna become,
it'll have to become a bigger part of this conversation,
even though we're seeing the early signs
in coding right now.
- We're wrapping up at one last quick question.
Can you give us a sneak preview of your next tweet?
What's top of mind that we should know about?
- Any ideas out there?
What should we talk about?
Anybody got anything?
>> Okay — don't collaborate on tweets with large audiences. That's a really important lesson.
>> Maybe that can be the tweet itself. >> We'll see how that one does. - No —
